title: How do you avoid "AI asset soup" when prototyping games?
author: Endgame_Dad
selftext:
Hey everyone,

I’m experimenting with a small side project: a chess-RPG / roguelike where every battle is a chess puzzle or endgame, instead of RNG-based fights.

The main goal of this project right now is rapid prototyping using AI - I’m using AI-generated art and assets to iterate quickly on gameplay and structure before committing to custom art or a fixed style.

Current gameplay loop is roughly:

* Enter a battle
* Solve a chess position (mate, tactic, or conversion)
* Win → get gold → buy upgrades → move forward

Prototype is here:  
👉 [https://endgameheroes.com](https://endgameheroes.com)

What I’d love feedback on specifically from an AI gamedev / pipeline perspective:

* Does this seem like a reasonable use of AI for early-stage prototyping?
* How do you personally keep visual consistency when using AI for fast iteration?
* Have you found good workflows (style guides, LoRAs, strict prompts, post-processing, etc.) to avoid the “AI asset soup” look in prototypes?

This is intentionally very early and rough - the goal right now is learning + validating the loop, not shipping or polishing.

Would love to hear how others here handle AI in the *prototype → validation → refinement* phase.

comments.author: macuseri686
comments.body:
This is exactly the problem I ran into early on with the game I built. The “AI asset soup” effect is real.

What worked for me was treating art generation as a **workflow problem**, not a prompt problem. When I was building my tower-defense game Age of Steam, I kept breaking visual consistency any time assets were generated in isolation, and even between different views of the same asset.

That’s actually why I built **GameLabs Studio (** [**https://gamelabstudio.co**](https://gamelabstudio.co) **).** It’s designed around a full workflow where style, perspective, and camera angle are enforced *across* all generated assets. You define the reference style once, and every image, animation, and spritesheet is generated against that same contract, so towers, enemies, and tiles always match.
